newsitem.title: INDIA: India relaxes rules for external borrowing.
newsitem.headline: India relaxes rules for external borrowing.

text.p: The Indian government on Friday liberalised rules for external borrowing of funds by corporates as well as for infrastructure projects, officials and analysts said.
"I see this probably as an outcome of the capital account convertibility report," Aashish Pitale, debt research manager at ICICI Securities and Finance Co, told Reuters.
A panel appointed by Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to chart the path of capital account convertibility had submitted its report earlier this month.
The panel set out certain pre-conditions and suggested making the rupee convertible on the capital account over the next three years.

The Finance Ministry has accepted one of the recommendations of the panel and decided to remove the ceiling on external commercial borrowings (ECBs) with average maturities of more than 10 years, officials said.
"Loans for period with average maturity of 10 years and above (have been kept) outside the external commercial borrowing (ECB) ceiling," a finance ministry statement said.
"However, the extent of debt raised under this window would be reviewed by the government periodically," it added.
The decision to relax rules on borrowing by corporates will spur firms to raise more funds from abroad, analysts said.
"The big players like Reliance, TELCO will be able to borrow more easily now," Pitale said.
To spur investment in infrastructure, the ministry also relaxed some curbs on ECBs for infrastructure and project financing.
It said in a statement that normally ECBs can account for up to 35 percent of the total cost of all infrastructure and greenfield projects.
"In case of telecom projects, 50 percent of the project cost (including the licence fee) will be allowed as a matter of course," the statement said.
It said that greater flexibility used to be allowed in the case of power projects. "Now it has been decided to extend this flexibility to other infrastructure projects also, on merit,"

The statement said that currently ECBs for project financing, or non-recourse financing, could carry a larger interest rate spread above the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) or U.S. Treasuries than ordinary ECBs.
"Ordinarily a spread of up to 350 basis points may be allowed," it said. "However, keeping market conditions in mind, some flexibility will be permitted in determining the spread on merit."
"The policies are a signal of the country's commitment to economic reforms," said a finance ministry official.
